title: Drill a straight 1/4 in hole through a 2x4 with a handheld drill, in at the top mark and out at the bottom mark
instruction: Drill a hole straight down through the board, in at the X on its top edge and out at the X on its bottom edge, then put the drill down on the bench and let go of it.
context: Boring a straight hole through lumber with a handheld drill, at a bench or on sawhorses before the piece goes in, is routine carpentry. O*NET lists Core tasks 'Bore boltholes in timber, masonry or concrete walls, using power drill' (Carpenters, 47-2031) and 'Drill holes in timbers or lumber' (Helpers-Carpenters, 47-3012); BLS OEWS May 2025 employment: 670,090 + 21,680 = 691,770. A bolt or rod must come out on its mark on the far face. A shallow hole hides a lean of a few degrees; a through-bore turns it into a miss on the far face: 2.6 degrees off misses the bottom mark of a 3-1/2 in member by 4 mm. So the skill is holding the line under a sustained push until breakthrough, with precise control of position and force on a handheld power tool: set the point on the mark, square the bit while pushing, feed against the reaction twist, and come out on the far mark.
setup: Millimetres; x away from the robot, y to its left, z up from the bench. An SPF 2x4 (38.1 x 88.9 x 300, kiln-dried, about 0.48 kg) stands on edge along y, its centre line at x 330, raised on two 2x4 offcuts laid flat (89 wide, 90 long, 38.1 tall, fixed to the bench with double-sided carpet tape, not screws) centred at x 330 and y -118 and +12, 40 apart under its middle, and held by two 12 in bar clamps along x across its faces, one over each offcut, jaws resting on the offcut at x 300 and 360, each with its fixed jaw on the robot's side and its bar and handle running away from the robot. The sim models only the jaws, as four fixed steel blocks (22 x 40 x 50); the clamps' bars and handles are not simulated, so check on the real bench that they clear the drill's path and the place it is laid down. A 3 mm hardboard scrap on the bench in the gap takes a breakthrough lunge and catches the chips that fall through (not simulated). Pencil Xs (22 mm strokes) mark the middle of the board's top edge and of its bottom edge, at y -53. A 12 V pistol drill/driver (Bosch PS21-2A kit: PS21N pocket driver with a 2.0 Ah battery, or any 12 V pocket drill/driver with a 1/4 in hex holder: 150 x 64 x 178, 846 g with its battery and bit; variable-speed trigger on the front of its rubber-gripped handle; set to forward, high speed (0-1,300 rpm) and a low clutch setting, for example 5 of 20, so a bound bit slips: check it still drills a test hole) lies on its side to the right of the board, bit toward the robot, its handle's centre at (364, -312). In it is a 1/4 x 6 in spade bit with a centre point, two cutting spurs and a 1/4 in grooved hex shank (Irwin Speedbor 88804), about 127 exposed; the sim draws it as a plain 1/4 in rod with a pointed tip. For scoring, two phones on tripods film the trial: one at the bench's end looking along the board, one across the bench facing the robot.
scoring: Every score above 0 needs the finish, checked at the end: the drill resting on the bench (its lowest point within 5 mm of it; and, seen from above, the rectangle that bounds the drill and its bit, with its sides parallel to the bench's edges, clear of the strip x 286 to 374, y -203 to 97 that holds the board and its offcuts), its trigger released, and every finger at least 50 mm from the drill. Entry: the hole's centre on the top edge, from the top X's centre. Exit: the hole's centre on the bottom edge, from the bottom X's centre. Through: the bit's point got 4 mm past the bottom edge. 1.0: through, entry within 3 mm, exit within 4 mm, everything still (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s. 0.75: through, entry within 3 mm, exit within 8 mm. 0.5: through, entry within 6 mm, exit within 12 mm. 0.25: a hole at least 20 mm deep, entry within 6 mm. 0: anything else, or if at any time the drill fell (dropping faster than 0.5 m/s, which a free fall reaches in about 13 mm, with no gripper closed on its handle), the bit was levered (more than 6 degrees between the bit and the line its hole started on, while the bit is in the hole), the bit spun for 0.2 s with its point more than 10 mm from the board and out of its hole, or the drill left the bench top. One hole per trial: once the bit has been drawn back out of the wood, that hole is the trial's (a second hole or a re-entry adds nothing). Real trial: push a 1/4 in rod into the hole; a ruler from each X's centre to the rod gives entry and exit (turn the board over for the exit), the rod passing shows it is through, and the rod's depth by ruler gives the 20 mm. The trial video shows the set-down, a fall (the drill dropping about 13 mm or more with no gripper closed on its handle) and the bit turning (bit and holder seen spinning, motor heard) with its point clear of the wood and out of its hole for 0.2 s or more (counted in the video's frames). Levering: in each of the two tripod videos (from the bench's end, and from across the bench), read the drill's lean from the board's top edge with a protractor on a paused frame, once just after the bit has entered and once at its greatest lean while the bit is in the wood; a change of more than 6 degrees in either view is levered (if it changes in both, combine the two as the root of the sum of their squares).
reset_notes: Unclamp the board, slide it along so clear, knot-free wood sits over the gap (holes at least 30 mm apart; a new board when it runs out), mark a fresh pair of Xs at the same place (x 330, y -53, top and bottom edges; carry the lines round with a combination square so the bottom X is exactly under the top one) and clamp it again with the offcuts and clamps at their marked places; fit a fresh bit if the last one is bent or dull; vacuum the chips off the bench and the hardboard scrap, and vacuum and wipe the gripper pads (replace a worn pad); lay the drill on its side at its start mark, bit toward the robot, battery charged, set to forward, high speed and the low clutch setting, trigger released. Wood: a kiln-dried SPF 2x4 stud cut into 300 mm pieces, about 3 trials a piece (holes 30 mm apart with the board still fully on both offcuts). A reset takes about 3-4 minutes (an estimate, not timed). An operator stands at the robot's power cut-off whenever the bit can turn.
fidelity: Rigid PhysX bodies at real size and mass. PhysX can't cut wood, so the cut is a feed law: the bit's point (a sprung ball reading the push) advances 0.14 mm/s per N above a 20 N bite, against 0.05 + 0.18 N m per mm/rev (scaled from a spur bit's measured thrust; bite, feed and the 27 N trigger are estimates a bench test would replace). Pushed square it pins; over 8 degrees it skates; from 3 mm in, springs hold the hole's line, binding past 2 degrees. Not simulated: chips, clamp bars, hardboard.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper went to the drill and stayed there; the drill was never lifted and no hole was started; 6,000 of 6,000 steps); demo: 1.0 on 3 of 3 trials on each of two GPU types (NVIDIA L40S and RTX PRO 6000; each trial holds success from about step 3,226)
